topic: multi-agent systems; literature sampling methodology; publication chronology
status: bounded chronology caveat observed in one three-record arXiv submission stratum; not a corpus-wide rate estimate
claim: In the sampled `agent_memory_coordination × 2010–2014` lexical-priority cell, two of three arXiv records are re-posted JAIR articles whose PDFs identify original publication years 2000 and 2002; only the third is a 2013 journal paper. Thus arXiv first-submission year is a useful repository-ingest stratum but is not a reliable proxy for when the research was published or conducted. Any historical trend using these bins should reconcile original venue/publication dates and keep preprint/repository-posting date separately.
positive_evidence: The `1106.0235v1` PDF front matter identifies JAIR volume 12 (2000), pp. 105–147, while its arXiv record was first submitted in 2011.
The `1106.4573v1` PDF front matter identifies JAIR volume 17 (2002), pp. 171–228, while its arXiv record was first submitted in 2011.
The third cell paper, `1312.4259v1`, is an IJACSA article from 2013, so the same arXiv stratum contains substantially different research eras.
counterevidence: A three-record lexical-priority cell is too small and purposive to estimate how often arXiv-date offsets occur across the 198,690-paper candidate pool.
The sampling frame deliberately uses arXiv submission date; its date bins remain internally valid for repository-availability sampling if they are not described as publication-year bins.
falsifiable_test: For a stratified sample across all topic-period cells, reconcile arXiv v1 submission date, earliest publicly verifiable manuscript date, and journal/conference publication date using paper front matter and authoritative venue metadata. Report offset distributions and recompute temporal analyses by both deposit year and publication year. The caveat weakens if offsets are negligible across a representative sample; it strengthens if multi-year offsets are common or cluster by subfield/venue. This batch does not estimate the corpus-wide frequency.
limitations: Only three purposively ranked records in one cell; venue/deposit metadata can be inconsistent and earliest research date is not always recoverable. No corpus-wide chronology audit was run in this batch.

topic: multi-agent systems; team monitoring; fault detection; coordination
status: conditional formal and empirical result from one sampled JAIR full text; no modern independent replication in this batch
claim: The sampled JAIR work reports that distributed socially-attentive monitoring can detect teamwork-relationship failures both soundly and completely while monitoring only key agents, under its simple-team and observability assumptions. Its analysis contrasts this with centralized monitoring that may trade soundness against completeness and may require monitoring every teammate. This is a positive result against an all-to-all-monitoring assumption, but not a guarantee for arbitrary multi-agent systems; the paper's own task-performance relation remains open.
positive_evidence: The paper states formal conditions under which distributed monitoring of a simple team with an observably partitioned team-plan set achieves sound and complete failure detection.
The article evaluates an implemented framework in two dynamic multi-agent domains, ModSAF and RoboCup-related settings, including online/offline monitoring and diagnosis.
The distributed monitor uses a single possibly incorrect hypothesis and monitors key agents rather than every teammate, distinguishing it from the more complex centralized method.
counterevidence: The theorem relies on explicit team and observability assumptions; the article notes that if key agents are unavailable, the distributed guarantee may lose either soundness or completeness.
The reported domains and plan representations do not cover arbitrary heterogeneous, networked, modern robot teams or asynchronous learned agents.
The article says correlation between its teamwork-quality feedback and task performance remains to be investigated; diagnostic correctness is not the same endpoint as mission success.

sources.sections: Sections 4–5 and Theorem 4 conditions; Sections 6–9 empirical applications and limitations

falsifiable_test: Reimplement the monitor on versioned cooperative-robot/team benchmarks and vary team hierarchy, key-agent availability, observation partitions, sensor noise, and communication loss. Against logged ground-truth team plans, report false-positive and false-negative rates, messages/bytes, latency, and task completion. The result generalizes if soundness/completeness and monitoring savings persist over held-out team structures; it is narrowed if realistic variants break either guarantee or erase resource savings. No system was reimplemented in this batch.
limitations: One 2000 JAIR paper selected through its 2011 arXiv deposit date; proof assumptions and historical simulation domains limit transfer. The result is a bounded model-level finding, not a universal claim or independent replication.

topic: multi-agent systems; adjustable autonomy; human-agent teams; decision transfer
status: bounded evidence synthesis from one sampled JAIR deployment paper and one targeted AAMAS full-text follow-up
claim: The 2002 adjustable-autonomy work documents a real E-Elves deployment with ten users over seven months and nearly 700 monitored meetings, while a 2009 follow-up evaluates continuous-time/interruptible policies in disaster-response simulation. The latter reports that RIAACT can improve team performance under some conditions but can underperform Always Accept when the estimated probability that resolving a human-agent inconsistency is useful is low. Therefore the open test is calibration and outcome robustness, not whether multi-step transfer strategies have ever been deployed or evaluated.
positive_evidence: The sampled JAIR paper reports E-Elves daily use by ten research-group users from June to December 2000, with nearly 700 meetings monitored, strategy diversity, and correspondence between MDP policies and model predictions.
The 2009 AAMAS RIAACT follow-up models continuous-time transfer, inconsistency resolution, and interruptible actions in an urban disaster-response simulation.
RIAACT reports averaged simulation results over 50 runs and a statistically significant comparison (reported p=0.0163) for one setting.
counterevidence: The E-Elves deployment is observational system-use evidence, not a randomized comparison proving causal user/task benefit; the paper's auction comparison covers only three dates.

RIAACT's benefit depends on P(IU), the probability that resolving a detected inconsistency improves the team decision; at P(IU)=0.3 the paper reports worse outcomes than Always Accept for a tested response-time distribution.
The follow-up uses simulation and assumed duration/utility distributions; it is not evidence that the same policy is superior with real users under every deadline or domain.

sources.sections: Sections 5.1, 5.3–5.4: E-Elves deployment, strategy observations and experiments

sources.title: Improving Adjustable Autonomy Strategies for Time-Critical Domains
sources.sections: Sections 4–5: disaster-response experiments, 50-run outcomes and P(IU) sensitivity

falsifiable_test: Prospectively estimate and calibrate P(IU) from past human/agent disagreements, then compare strategy-based control with Always Accept, Always Autonomous, and timeout-only baselines in matched time-critical tasks. Sweep error in P(IU), response-time distributions, task deadlines, interruption costs, and team size; report mission/task reward, completion, latency, human burden, and failures with uncertainty intervals. The lead weakens if the strategy remains uniformly better when P(IU) is poorly calibrated or shows no benefit when calibrated; it strengthens if a measurable calibration threshold predicts the point where delegation helps. No user or disaster-response study was run here.
limitations: Two related studies from the same research community and different settings/endpoints; the 2002 field deployment does not isolate causal effect, and the 2009 evidence is a simulation. This is not a general comparative-effectiveness estimate.

topic: multi-agent systems; Contract Net Protocol; dynamic task allocation
status: bounded evaluation-design lead from one sampled 2013 full text and one targeted, distinct 2019 ICNP full text
claim: The sampled 2013 updated-CNP paper implements in-flight task changes in a five-task predator–prey case with two changes and compares JADE/FIPA-ACL and JATLite/KQML, but its own future work calls for application-specific and scalability studies. A 2019 paper reports larger Repast task-assignment experiments for a different pheromone/response-threshold/re-forwarding ICNP, including 100% completion at 30 agents/1,000 tasks/Lmax=3 versus 86.7% for classical CNP and 93.2% for DCNP. That adjacent evidence shows larger-scale CNP variants have been studied, but does not validate the 2013 in-flight task-change rule. Shared ‘improved CNP’ labels are not evidence that protocol mechanisms or outcomes are interchangeable.
positive_evidence: The 2013 paper implements task modification during contractor execution in two agent platforms and two communication languages; it reports qualitative faster accommodation in the five-task/two-change example.
The 2019 Algorithms paper compares its distinct ICNP with classical and dynamic CNP over simulated settings varying task counts (50–1,000) and agent counts (10–50).
At 30 agents, 1,000 tasks and maximum load 3, the 2019 paper reports 133 classical-CNP errors/86.7% completion, 68 DCNP errors/93.2%, and 11 ICNP errors successfully re-forwarded/100% completion.
counterevidence: The 2013 case varies platform and communication language, offering some implementation diversity even though the workload has only five tasks and two changed tasks.
The 2019 ICNP uses pheromone/response thresholds and re-forwarding, not the same task-modification rule; its result cannot be treated as a replication or direct contradiction.

The 2019 authors acknowledge redundant shared-environment information may reduce contractor efficiency and identify collaborative bidding/assignment constraints as future work; both studies are simulated rather than broad production deployments.

sources.sections: Section IV and results: predator–prey setup, five tasks/two changes, platform/language comparisons; future work

sources.title: Task Assignment of the Improved Contract Net Protocol under a Multi-Agent System
sources.sections: Sections 4–5 and Table 2: Repast study, task/agent scaling, classical/DCNP/ICNP comparisons; Section 6 limitations

falsifiable_test: Implement updated-CNP and the 2019 pheromone/threshold ICNP beside classical and dynamic CNP on preregistered dynamic workloads with changing task requirements, arrivals, agent failures, and heterogeneous agent capability. Match compute/message budgets; measure bytes/messages, elapsed time, task utility, completion, reallocation error, fairness, and deadlock across seeds and sizes; publish code/workloads. The lead strengthens if the 2013 task-change rule improves these endpoints under held-out application workloads beyond same-mechanism baselines; it weakens if its benefit disappears under matched budgets or other CNP variants dominate. No protocol was reimplemented in this batch.
limitations: One small 2013 case study and one distinct 2019 synthetic ICNP evaluation; neither is an independent replication of the other mechanism. No source code, raw results, or statistical replication of the 2013 graph outcomes was audited here.
